doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Six months in Spain and the government's reaction
summary: He waited six months for papers, wrote for the Finnish radio orchestra and played a Madrid jazz club; Cuban officials took his wife's car and warned her never to leave, and the marriage fell apart.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: How long did you stay in Spain?
Six months, I stay in Spain.
That’s how long it took to process your papers?
And what happened after your papers were processed?

I came to New York. Well, before that I wrote some music for the Finnish Radio Orchestra. I had a friend there called Esko Linnaveli who used to be the conductor the big band there. So he commissioned me some arrangements.

To help me out, yea. And, I work with a group of South American musicians [in Madrid]; that was my first professional Latin Jazz gig. The whole week we in a called Dahlia’s Club, was a Jazz club. So, they help; there they pay me a salary in that place. Then I came here after six months.
What was your sense of the Cuban government’s response to your defection?
Did they try to contact you? Paquito:No, they never tried to contact me.
Yes; they contact my wife, directly from, the Minister of Culture. And first of all they took my car from my wife—

Took the car; you are not going to have the car anymore, and they told her not to ever try to, never intend to leave the country, because you are never going to be able to leave the country, never. So, try to remake your life here, because we are not going to allow you to leave the country. So, it look like she believe that, because after a year or something, the marriage fall apart, and we, I never gave her the divorce, because if I sign the divorce is going to be harder for her to come to this country, to leave the country.
